newsitem.title: INDIA: India has minerals, needs funds, know-how--study.
newsitem.headline: India has minerals, needs funds, know-how--study.

text.p: India needs an effective strategy, adequate funds and modern technology to exploit fully its vast mineral deposits, analysts at a mining conference said on Sunday.

India's central region, comprising five states and spread over 1.36 million square km (510,000 sq miles), accounts for the bulk of the country's mineral production, said two analysts who presented the results of a recent study.

This includes 87 percent of India's coal, 92 percent of its bauxite, 75 percent of its copper ores, 82 percent of its iron ore, 49 percent of its manganese ore and 99 percent of its chromite, the study said.
Yet the region has not been exploited to its maximum.

"This region still has huge potential of several mineral resources which have yet to be tapped to the fullest," said S.V. Ali, controller of mines, and M. Brahmanandan, a senior economist with the Indian Bureau of Mining.
The analysts called for increased investment in the exploration and development of the region.

"The recent discovery of high-value minerals like gold, diamonds, tungsten, etc. in this region, calls for investment for detailed exploration and development of these minerals," the analysts' study said.
The five states which account for the bulk of India's mineral wealth are Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and Bihar.
The study said India's liberalised mining policy and recent amendments to mining laws could help develop these reserves.
India opened the mining sector to private and foreign investment in March 1993 as part of an economic reforms programme initiated two years earlier.
The study said exploration carried out for diamonds so far did not yield any commercial prospects in the primary kimberlites in Madhya Pradesh.
"But application of the most sophisticated aeromagentic and geochemical survey backed by investment can possibly lead to the discovery of new diamond sources," the study said.
India is the world's largest exporter of cut and polished diamonds, although its domestic resources are negligible.
It annually imports around 70 million carats of rough diamonds to meet the requirements of the cutting and polishing industry. Its domestic production is only 30,000 carats.
India's gold production is also negligible while its annual consumption at 500 tonnes, including 300 tonnes of imports and 200 tonnnes of recycled metal, is the world's highest.

Exploration for gold has revealed only small deposits up to shallow depths in southern India. The exploration has been conventional, with limited inputs from geophysics, geochemistry and remote sensing.
Recently gold occurrences have been identified in Orissa, Bihar and Maharashtra in central India.
"Modern geochemical methods in the greenstone areas of central India hold strong possiblities for discovering gold deposits," the study said.

The study said the availability of limestone in central India had helped the country emerge as one of the world's major producers of cement. Cement-grade limestone deposits in the central region have been estimated at 1,700 million tonnes.
"The availability of coal in central India, along with other raw materials such as clay, can give a fillip to the establishment of new cement plants," the study said.
